The Foundation for Food & Agriculture Research and Entomol Products, LLC are investing $448,940 in a Rapid Outcomes from Agricultural Research or ROAR grant to test an innovative, plant-based approach to reduce transmission of avian influenza. Researchers are determining whether intermittently fogging or misting hydrogenated catmint oil (HCO), a product with demonstrated antiviral properties, in poultry housing can interrupt transmission of avian influenza viruses. Avian influenza has severe economic consequences for the U.S. poultry and egg industries. The virus spreads rapidly among birds and leads to mass depopulation of infected flocks. This influenza virus is classified as high or low pathogenic avian influenza based on how it affects poultry. Highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses cause severe disease and high mortality in infected poultry, while low pathogenic avian influenza is a mild or asymptomatic viral infection. “Producers need practical solutions to reduce avian influenza transmission that work with existing infrastructure to protect their flocks and limit losses,” said Dr. Jasmine Bruno, FFAR scientific program director. “As fogging is a widely used practice in poultry houses, we want to know if it’s a promising mechanism for protecting birds.” TESTING HCO HCO is a modified plant essential oil and an EPA-registered active ingredient used in commercially available insect repellents. Previous research found that aerosolized formulations containing HCO significantly reduced H1N1 influenza virus in the air. Led by Dr. David Hallahan, chief science officer at Entomol, and Dr. Ekramy Sayedahmed, assistant professor of poultry medicine at Purdue University, researchers are testing whether HCO can reduce avian influenza transmission. The researchers are using low pathogenic avian influenza to evaluate HCO’s antiviral effects against avian influenza and inform its potential application against highly pathogenic avian influenza. The team is also establishing effective aerosol delivery parameters, including HCO concentration, fogging duration and frequency, effective range and overall efficacy. “Entomol’s hydrogenated catmint oil technology has demonstrated the ability to disrupt influenza viruses in the air and on surfaces at very low concentrations, said Dr. Hallahan. “This FFAR-supported project will allow us to rigorously evaluate its potential as a practical biosecurity tool for poultry producers.” FFAR is investing in this research to support the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s research priority on increasing profitability of farmers and ranchers. This research aims to develop a practical, science-driven intervention that strengthens national readiness for avian influenza outbreaks and protects U.S. poultry producers’ livelihoods. FFAR’s ROAR program rapidly funds research and outreach in response to emerging or unanticipated threats to the U.S. food supply or agricultural systems. Thursday, September 24, 2026 Virus Research: Genetic Diversity of Clade 2.3.4.4b H5Nx High Pathogenicity Avian Influenza Viruses Detected in Korea During the 2025–2026 Winter Season and Pathogenicity of H5N1 and H5N9 Viruses #19,347 Last December - in addition to reporting numerous biosecurity breaches on farms - South Korea's MAFRA Reported Increased Infectivity & Pathogenicity of This Year's Avian Flu Strains, which - for the first time - included 3 HPAI strains (H5N1, H5N6, and H5N9). Of particular concern, their Animal and Plant Quarantine Agency conducted an evaluation of the infectivity and pathogenicity of one highly pathogenic avian influenza virus (serotype H5N1) and found that the infectivity was more than 10 times higher than in previous years. Details at the time were understandably scant, but today we've a research article which sheds new light on the panoply of viruses behind last year's difficult avian flu season in South Korea. While this is a fairly technical report, and the use of regional nomenclature for H5N1 genotypes further complicates matters, the gist is pretty simple. Last year South Korea was visited by a diverse panoply of H5Nx genotypes (n=16), with at least two - H5N9 N9-G2 and H5N1 25G2 - displaying unusually high infectivity in chickens. H5N1 25G2 was also deadly to ducks, whereas H5N9 N9-G2 spread efficiently in ducks, albeit without producing serious illness. H5N1 25G2 was the source of nearly half (n=30) of last year's 62 South Korean poultry outbreaks, but it was only detected in environmental samples once, making its prevalence in wild birds unknown. Whether 25G2 (or H5N9 N9-G2) will return to South Korea this fall - or turn up in other regions - remains to be seen. Due to its technical nature, I've only provided the link, abstract, and a few excerpts. Follow the link to read the report in its entirety. Genetic Diversity of Clade 2.3.4.4b H5Nx High Pathogenicity Avian Influenza Viruses Detected in Korea During the 2025–2026 Winter Season and Pathogenicity of H5N1 and H5N9 Viruses Yunyueng Jang, Ra Mi Cha, Min-Ji Park, Jong-Min Kim, Eui Hyeon Lim, Gyeong-Beom Heo, Se-Hee An, Bina Lee, Hyun-ji Seo, Kwang-Nyeong Lee, Youn-Jeong Lee, Eun-Kyoung Lee 10.1016/j.virusres.2026.199807 PDF Highlights During 2025-2026, clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1, H5N6, and H5N9 HPAIVs were detected in Korea, causing 62 H5Nx HPAI outbreaks in poultry, and 63 cases in wild birds. Ten genotypes (24G1, 25G2–25G7, and N9-G1–3) identified in poultry, among which 25G2 was the dominant genotype. Most genotypes were reassortants containing gene segments derived from East Asian clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 HPAIVs since 2022 and LPAIVs from wild birds. The 25G2 and N9-G2 genotype showed high infectivity in chickens with 103.3 and 103.2 EID50 of LD50 values, respectively. The 25G2 caused rapid duck mortality, whereas H5N9 caused asymptomatic infection with efficient transmission. ABSTRACT Clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1, H5N6, and H5N9 high pathogenicity avian influenza viruses (HPAIVs) were detected in poultry and wild birds during the 2025–2026 winter season in Korea. During this period, 62 H5Nx HPAI outbreaks occurred in poultry, and 63 cases were reported in wild birds. Genome constellation analysis revealed substantial genotype diversity. Most H5N1 and H5N9 genotypes were reassortants containing gene segments derived from East Asian clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 HPAIVs since 2022 and low-pathogenicity avian influenza viruses from wild birds. Notably, the European H5N1 genotype EA-2024-DI.2.1, which spread rapidly across Europe in 2025, and its reassortants were identified in Korea. The novel poultry genotypes were also detected in wild birds, supporting wild bird to poultry spillover, whereas one genotype detected in previous season was identified in small-scale poultry farms. H5N1 (C588) of major 25G2 genotype in poultry and H5N9 (C722) of N9-G2 genotype showed high infectivity in chickens with 103.3 and 103.2 EID50 of median lethal dose (LD50) values, respectively. The predominance of the 25G2 genotype in poultry may have been influenced by efficient infection and virus introduction into high-density poultry production areas, potentially facilitating horizontal transmission under field conditions. In young ducks, H5N1 caused rapid mortality, whereas H5N9 induced limited clinical signs without mortality. Both viruses were transmitted to all contact ducks, increasing the risk of transmission to poultry. Despite intensified surveillance and early detection efforts to limit virus spread, H5Nx HPAIV outbreaks occurred during the 2025–2026 winter season. These findings highlight the need for continued surveillance, together with rapid genomic and pathogenic characterization of newly introduced viruses. (SNIP) Genotype 25G2 was the predominant genotype detected in poultry during the 2025–2026 season, accounting for 30 outbreaks. However, it was identified in only one environmental sample collected during an epidemiological investigation of migratory bird habitats. This outbreak pattern differed from those observed during previous seasons in Korea, in which the predominant genotypes were generally similar between wild birds and poultry (Cha et al., 2023; Cha et al., 2025; Cha et al., 2026). The predominance of genotype 25G2 in poultry may have been influenced by higher infectivity under field conditions, particularly in layer farms located in high-density poultry farming areas where HPAI outbreaks were concentrated. However, introduction through environmental contamination associated with wild birds cannot be excluded, and the potential influence of sampling bias resulting from spatial and temporal variations in bird migration and surveillance should also be considered (Hayes et al., 2025; Llanos-Soto, Yaffy, Pavlak and Ivanek, 2025). This study revealed multiple introductions of genetically diverse H5 viruses during the 2025–2026 winter season and demonstrated their relatively high infectivity in chickens. Epidemiological investigations of concurrent outbreaks, together with virus detection and genetic analyses, helped identify potential sources of virus introduction in the affected regions and provided evidence of viral contamination in the surrounding environment. Despite enhanced surveillance and early detection efforts to limit virus spread, H5 HPAI outbreaks still occurred in poultry farms. These findings highlight the importance of continued surveillance in wild birds and poultry, coupled with the rapid genomic and pathogenic characterization of newly emerging viruses, to support the implementation of effective avian influenza control disease. (Continue . . . ) ECDC/EFSA Quarterly Avian Influenza Overview June-August 2026 2025-2026: HPAI's Biggest Surge in Wild Birds to Date (Europe) #19,346 As the above EDC/EFSA chart illustrates, after a couple of lackluster years (2023-2025) avian flu returned to Europe with a vengeance last year. We saw similar upticks in places like South Korea, and North America, but reporting from large swaths of the world - particularly in Asia and Africa - is often lacking (see FAO graphic below). Every 3 months the ECDC/EFSA publishes a highly detailed avian influenza surveillance report, and while they tend to be EU centric, in its 67 pages you'll find ample coverage of outbreaks and infections from around the world on a wide variety of avian subtypes. While today's report covers the slowest part (June-August) of the year, these highly detailed quarterly reports make excellent reference material, and are well worth perusing. This edition does contain one milestone, however; the long-dreaded arrival of HPAI to Australia/New Zealand, which was first reported in June. I've posted the Abstract, and a few excerpts below. I'll have a brief postscript after the break. Abstract Between 5 June and 28 August 2026, 110 highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N1) virus detections were reported in domestic (7) and wild (103) birds in 12 countries in Europe.The number of detections remained at a seasonal low throughout the summer, continuing the decline observed since spring. In contrast to previous years, fewer colony-breeding seabirds were affected, and the geographical range of detections was more limited. Further sporadic detections of HPAI A(H5) virus were reported in wild terrestrial carnivores and pinnipeds. Outside Europe, the epidemic continued in the Americas, where also the HPAI A(H7N3) subtype was detected in Mexico. Following its first introduction to mainland Australia, HPAI A(H5N1) virus spread within local wild bird populations and spilled over to terrestrial carnivores and marine mammals. In the US, the number of dairy cattle farms reportedly affected by HPAI A(H5N1) increased, while detections in captive American minks were reported for the first time. Between 5 June and 31 August 2026, 15 cases of avian influenza virus infection were publicly reported in humans (no fatal cases) in three countries and territories: Bangladesh (one A(H5N1) case), Cambodia (one A(H5N1) case) and China (13 A(H9N2) cases). All human cases reported exposure to poultry or a poultry environment prior to detection or onset of illness. Human infections with avian influenza viruses remain rare and no sustained human-to-human transmission has been documented. The risk posed by avian influenza A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b viruses currently circulating in Europe remains low for the general public in the European Union/European Economic Area (EU/EEA) and low-to-moderate for those occupationally or otherwise exposed to infected animals or contaminated environments. ©2026 European Food Safety Authority, European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control,European Union Reference Laboratory for Avian Influenza. EFSA Journal published by Wiley-VCH GmbH on behalf of European Food Safety Authority (Continued . . . ) As the chart at the top of this blog indicates, each avian flu season (which runs Oct 1st -Sept 30th) is different, sometimes punctuated by the arrival of new subtypes or genotypes, and often varying in intensity. As we go into a new fall season, migratory birds in the Northern Hemisphere are expected to bring with them a new wave of HPAI from their high-latitude breeding grounds (see H5Nx: Reassort & Repeat). While we can't know what kind of avian flu season lies ahead, now would be a good time to review the things you can do to lower your (currently, low) risk of exposure. WHO Interim Guidance to Reduce the Risk of Infection in People Exposed to Avian Influenza Viruses Backyard Flock Owners: Protect Yourself from Bird Flu (CDC Guidance) UF/IFAS Extension: What Backyard Flock Owners Need to Know about Bird Flu (Influenza H5N1) Wednesday, September 23, 2026 EM&I: Limited added benefit of seasonal influenza vaccination before A(H5) vaccination in mice and ferrets challenged with A(H5N1) Credit ACIP/CDC #19,345 One of the biggest challenges during any future H5Nx pandemic would be the rapid production and timely deployment of a two-dose (given 30 days apart) H5 vaccine to billions of people (see Referral: SCI AM - A Bird Flu Vaccine Might Come Too Late to Save Us from H5N1). While it's not a new idea (see 2008's Seasonal Flu Vaccine May Offer Some Protection To H5N1), the notion of using the existing seasonal flu vaccine as either a `stop-gap measure' - or as a `prime-boost' for the first pandemic jab, during the opening months of an H5 pandemic - has persisted. An early, encouraging 2010 study in the journal Vaccines (Seasonal influenza vaccine elicits heterosubtypic immunity against H5N1 that can be further boosted by H5N1 vaccination) reported: Recent findings indicate that seasonal influenza vaccination or infection of healthy humans may contribute to heterosubtypic immunity against new influenza A subtypes, such as H5N1. Here, we investigated whether seasonal influenza vaccination in a mouse model could induce any immunity against the H5N1 subtype. It could be demonstrated that, largely due to the H1N1 component strain A/NewCaledonia/20/99, parenteral immunization of mice with a trivalent seasonal influenza vaccine elicited heterosubtype H5-reactive antibodies able to confer partial protection against H5N1 influenza virus infection. Furthermore, the trivalent seasonal influenza vaccine was found to be compatible with a whole virus H5N1 vaccine in a heterologous prime-boost immunization regimen, achieving superior efficacy compared to a single immunization with an equivalent low-dose of the H5N1 vaccine. More recent evidence remains both mixed and modest - and has often relied on ferret or mouse models (which may not fully apply to humans) - including: Nature Comms: Adjuvanted Influenza Vaccination Increases Pre-existing H5N1 Cross-reactive Antibodies mBio: Low levels of influenza H5N1 HA and NA antibodies in the human population are boosted by seasonal H1N1 infection but not by H3N2 infection or influenza vaccination EID Journal: Effect of Seasonal Influenza Vaccines on Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Clade 2.3.4.4b Virus Infection in Ferrets EID Journal: Investigation of Influenza A(H5N1) Virus Neutralization by Quadrivalent Seasonal Vaccines, United Kingdom, 2021–2024 Note: Regardless of whether the seasonal flu vaccine directly protects against H5N1 infection, there are still good reasons to get the jab, prior to - and even during - an H5Nx pandemic. It still may provide some small boost to your immune response. Neutralizing antibodies aren't the only immune defense against infection. It could help prevent a co-infection with H5N1 and seasonal flu, which has the potential for being more severe. Co-infections could also help generate a reassorted `hybrid' virus (see Preprint: Intelligent Prediction & Biological Validation of the High Reassortment Potential of Avian H5N1 and Human H3N2 Influenza Viruses). While it may not be the last word on the topic, today we've a study in EM&I from researchers at the CDC's NCIRD Influenza Division, which frankly, offers little encouragement on the effectiveness of using seasonal flu vaccines as a `prime-boost' for H5N1 vaccines. I've only reproduced the abstract and a few excerpts, so follow the link to read the report in its entirety. I'll have a brief postscript after the break. Limited added benefit of seasonal influenza vaccination before A(H5) vaccination in mice and ferrets challenged with A(H5N1) Masato Hatta , Ying Huang , Jeremy A. Duke , Joseph R. Rouse , Chenchen Feng , Xudong Lin , show all Article: 2731495 | Received 29 Jun 2026, Accepted 05 Sep 2026, Published online: 21 Sep 2026 https://doi.org/10.1080/22221751.2026.2731495 Limited A(H5)-specific vaccine supply is expected early in a potential A(H5N1) pandemic, raising the question of whether licensed seasonal influenza vaccines could enhance protection when administered before A(H5) vaccination. We evaluated this strategy in mouse and ferret models using clade 2.3.4.4b A(H5N1) viruses. Seasonal influenza vaccination induced antibodies to seasonal haemagglutinins but did not induce detectable antibodies against A(H5) and did not consistently enhance A(H5)-directed antibody responses after A(H5) vaccination. In lethal challenge studies, seasonal vaccine priming before A(H5) vaccination was associated with improved outcomes compared with A(H5) vaccination alone in one of three mouse experiments, but this effect was not observed in the other two mouse experiments or in ferrets. These findings suggest that seasonal influenza vaccine priming provides limited added benefit to A(H5) vaccine-mediated protection against A(H5N1) under the conditions tested. (SNIP) Accordingly, clinical studies are needed to further evaluate the strategy of administering seasonal influenza vaccine prior to A(H5) vaccination. However, such studies would likely rely on immunological endpoints rather than direct assessment of protection. Evidence of cross-reactivity alone should therefore be interpreted cautiously when informing decision-making, as it may not reliably predict protection against severe or lethal A(H5N1) infection. In the absence of a clear added benefit, prioritizing seasonal influenza vaccination as a priming strategy to enhance protection against A(H5N1) during the early phase of a pandemic may offer limited value, particularly when resources may need to be directed toward A(H5)-specific vaccination and other countermeasures. Continued efforts to improve the development, availability, and deployment of antigenically similar A(H5) vaccines should remain a priority for pandemic preparedness [13,14]. (Continue . . . ) Although the prospect of using seasonal vaccine as a bridge - or as a primer for a first H5 dose - remains biologically plausible, the evidence of its effectiveness has been both inconsistent and weak. Today's CDC study reports that prior seasonal vaccination offered little reproducible improvement over H5 vaccination alone (at least, in mice and ferrets). While disappointing, it is hardly unexpected. Which suggests that during the opening months of any novel flu pandemic we will (once again) have to rely on NPIs (Non-pharmaceutical Interventions) like social distancing and face masks - and our limited supply of antivirals - while a strain-specific vaccine is produced and deployed. For some specific preparedness advice, you may wish to revisit #Natlprep 2026: Pandemic Planning At Both Ends of the Spectrum. [KATERYNA KON/Science Photo Library/Getty Images] With flu season ramping up in certain areas of the world (it’s time to get that flu shot!) everyone is watching what strains are circulating—and how well they may match the current vaccine formulations. Some strains are watched more closely than others, and the highly pathogenic avian H5N1, a subtype of the influenza A virus that causes avian influenza (“bird flu”), may garner the most attention as it is regarded as one of the largest pandemic threats. Although H5N1 primarily infects birds, it can also infect mammals. Human infections are uncommon and have generally occurred after close contact with infected animals or contaminated environments. The World Health Organization reports no sustained person-to-person transmission. The Global Virus Network (GVN) is closely monitoring detections of H5N1 in several mammal species in Australia as the virus continues to spread. Last week, Australian authorities confirmed the first detection in an Australian sea lion, an endangered species, at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island. Australia reported its first confirmed detection in a mammal on August 23, when a long-nosed fur seal found at Beachport in South Australia tested positive. A second long-nosed fur seal near Kangaroo Island was confirmed two days later and subsequent detections included red foxes and a common dolphin. Australian authorities report no evidence of mammal-to-mammal transmission of the virus in Australia. The detections show the virus infecting several mammal species in Australia within weeks of its first reported appearance in the country’s wildlife. Globally, H5N1 has infected a growing range of mammals, including seals and other marine mammals, dairy cattle, cats and wild carnivores. Scientists are monitoring these infections for changes in the virus and evidence of transmission between mammals. “Given what we have seen with this H5N1 genotype in seal and sea lion populations overseas, a spillover into Australian marine mammals was a possibility we had been concerned about and actively monitoring for,” said Michelle Wille, PhD, an avian influenza researcher affiliated with the University of Melbourne and the WHO Collaborating Centre for Reference and Research on Influenza and the Peter Doherty Institute for Infection and Immunity, a GVN Center of Excellence in Australia. “While it is sobering to see that possibility become a reality, the priority now is detailed genomic analysis of this and any future detections. We need to closely monitor for mutations associated with better adaptation to mammals and determine whether infections represent separate spillover events from birds or evidence of transmission between seals. That distinction will be critical to understanding the risk posed by the virus as it continues to circulate in wildlife.” Australia first detected H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b in wild seabirds in June. The virus has since been found in wild birds across several parts of the country. As of September 17, Australia had reported 576 confirmed events in wildlife, including mass mortality events in greater crested terns. An event may involve one or more animals. In April 2025, GVN published an analysis in The Lancet Regional Health—Americas calling for stronger surveillance, biosecurity, genomic monitoring and preparedness as H5N1 spread. In April 2026, GVN issued a statement on H5N1 vaccine developments, emphasizing the need for continued vaccine development and broader pandemic preparedness. “Australia is another reminder that H5N1 is a global animal health issue with implications for human health that we need to continue watching closely,” said Sten H. Vermund, MD, PhD, GVN’s chief medical officer and dean of the University of South Florida College of Public Health. “There is no reason for alarm, but there is every reason to remain vigilant. Surveillance across species, rapid genomic analysis and open sharing of what we learn give us the best chance to recognize an important change in the virus early.” News Birds Epidemiology Genome analysis Genotype Influenza Influenza vaccine Mammals

Thursday, September 24, 2026 Virus Research: Genetic Diversity of Clade 2.3.4.4b H5Nx High Pathogenicity Avian Influenza Viruses Detected in Korea During the 2025–2026 Winter Season and Pathogenicity of H5N1 and H5N9 Viruses #19,347 Last December - in addition to reporting numerous biosecurity breaches on farms - South Korea's MAFRA Reported Increased Infectivity & Pathogenicity of This Year's Avian Flu Strains, which - for the first time - included 3 HPAI strains (H5N1, H5N6, and H5N9). Of particular concern, their Animal and Plant Quarantine Agency conducted an evaluation of the infectivity and pathogenicity of one highly pathogenic avian influenza virus (serotype H5N1) and found that the infectivity was more than 10 times higher than in previous years. Details at the time were understandably scant, but today we've a research article which sheds new light on the panoply of viruses behind last year's difficult avian flu season in South Korea. While this is a fairly technical report, and the use of regional nomenclature for H5N1 genotypes further complicates matters, the gist is pretty simple. Last year South Korea was visited by a diverse panoply of H5Nx genotypes (n=16), with at least two - H5N9 N9-G2 and H5N1 25G2 - displaying unusually high infectivity in chickens. H5N1 25G2 was also deadly to ducks, whereas H5N9 N9-G2 spread efficiently in ducks, albeit without producing serious illness. H5N1 25G2 was the source of nearly half (n=30) of last year's 62 South Korean poultry outbreaks, but it was only detected in environmental samples once, making its prevalence in wild birds unknown. Whether 25G2 (or H5N9 N9-G2) will return to South Korea this fall - or turn up in other regions - remains to be seen. Due to its technical nature, I've only provided the link, abstract, and a few excerpts. Follow the link to read the report in its entirety. Genetic Diversity of Clade 2.3.4.4b H5Nx High Pathogenicity Avian Influenza Viruses Detected in Korea During the 2025–2026 Winter Season and Pathogenicity of H5N1 and H5N9 Viruses Yunyueng Jang, Ra Mi Cha, Min-Ji Park, Jong-Min Kim, Eui Hyeon Lim, Gyeong-Beom Heo, Se-Hee An, Bina Lee, Hyun-ji Seo, Kwang-Nyeong Lee, Youn-Jeong Lee, Eun-Kyoung Lee 10.1016/j.virusres.2026.199807 PDF Highlights During 2025-2026, clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1, H5N6, and H5N9 HPAIVs were detected in Korea, causing 62 H5Nx HPAI outbreaks in poultry, and 63 cases in wild birds. Ten genotypes (24G1, 25G2–25G7, and N9-G1–3) identified in poultry, among which 25G2 was the dominant genotype. Most genotypes were reassortants containing gene segments derived from East Asian clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 HPAIVs since 2022 and LPAIVs from wild birds. The 25G2 and N9-G2 genotype showed high infectivity in chickens with 103.3 and 103.2 EID50 of LD50 values, respectively. The 25G2 caused rapid duck mortality, whereas H5N9 caused asymptomatic infection with efficient transmission. ABSTRACT Clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1, H5N6, and H5N9 high pathogenicity avian influenza viruses (HPAIVs) were detected in poultry and wild birds during the 2025–2026 winter season in Korea. During this period, 62 H5Nx HPAI outbreaks occurred in poultry, and 63 cases were reported in wild birds. Genome constellation analysis revealed substantial genotype diversity. Most H5N1 and H5N9 genotypes were reassortants containing gene segments derived from East Asian clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 HPAIVs since 2022 and low-pathogenicity avian influenza viruses from wild birds. Notably, the European H5N1 genotype EA-2024-DI.2.1, which spread rapidly across Europe in 2025, and its reassortants were identified in Korea. The novel poultry genotypes were also detected in wild birds, supporting wild bird to poultry spillover, whereas one genotype detected in previous season was identified in small-scale poultry farms. H5N1 (C588) of major 25G2 genotype in poultry and H5N9 (C722) of N9-G2 genotype showed high infectivity in chickens with 103.3 and 103.2 EID50 of median lethal dose (LD50) values, respectively. The predominance of the 25G2 genotype in poultry may have been influenced by efficient infection and virus introduction into high-density poultry production areas, potentially facilitating horizontal transmission under field conditions. In young ducks, H5N1 caused rapid mortality, whereas H5N9 induced limited clinical signs without mortality. Both viruses were transmitted to all contact ducks, increasing the risk of transmission to poultry. Despite intensified surveillance and early detection efforts to limit virus spread, H5Nx HPAIV outbreaks occurred during the 2025–2026 winter season. These findings highlight the need for continued surveillance, together with rapid genomic and pathogenic characterization of newly introduced viruses. (SNIP) Genotype 25G2 was the predominant genotype detected in poultry during the 2025–2026 season, accounting for 30 outbreaks. However, it was identified in only one environmental sample collected during an epidemiological investigation of migratory bird habitats. This outbreak pattern differed from those observed during previous seasons in Korea, in which the predominant genotypes were generally similar between wild birds and poultry (Cha et al., 2023; Cha et al., 2025; Cha et al., 2026). The predominance of genotype 25G2 in poultry may have been influenced by higher infectivity under field conditions, particularly in layer farms located in high-density poultry farming areas where HPAI outbreaks were concentrated. However, introduction through environmental contamination associated with wild birds cannot be excluded, and the potential influence of sampling bias resulting from spatial and temporal variations in bird migration and surveillance should also be considered (Hayes et al., 2025; Llanos-Soto, Yaffy, Pavlak and Ivanek, 2025). This study revealed multiple introductions of genetically diverse H5 viruses during the 2025–2026 winter season and demonstrated their relatively high infectivity in chickens. Epidemiological investigations of concurrent outbreaks, together with virus detection and genetic analyses, helped identify potential sources of virus introduction in the affected regions and provided evidence of viral contamination in the surrounding environment. Despite enhanced surveillance and early detection efforts to limit virus spread, H5 HPAI outbreaks still occurred in poultry farms. These findings highlight the importance of continued surveillance in wild birds and poultry, coupled with the rapid genomic and pathogenic characterization of newly emerging viruses, to support the implementation of effective avian influenza control disease. (Continue . . . ) ECDC/EFSA Quarterly Avian Influenza Overview June-August 2026 2025-2026: HPAI's Biggest Surge in Wild Birds to Date (Europe) #19,346 As the above EDC/EFSA chart illustrates, after a couple of lackluster years (2023-2025) avian flu returned to Europe with a vengeance last year. We saw similar upticks in places like South Korea, and North America, but reporting from large swaths of the world - particularly in Asia and Africa - is often lacking (see FAO graphic below). Every 3 months the ECDC/EFSA publishes a highly detailed avian influenza surveillance report, and while they tend to be EU centric, in its 67 pages you'll find ample coverage of outbreaks and infections from around the world on a wide variety of avian subtypes. While today's report covers the slowest part (June-August) of the year, these highly detailed quarterly reports make excellent reference material, and are well worth perusing. This edition does contain one milestone, however; the long-dreaded arrival of HPAI to Australia/New Zealand, which was first reported in June. I've posted the Abstract, and a few excerpts below. I'll have a brief postscript after the break. Abstract Between 5 June and 28 August 2026, 110 highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N1) virus detections were reported in domestic (7) and wild (103) birds in 12 countries in Europe.The number of detections remained at a seasonal low throughout the summer, continuing the decline observed since spring. In contrast to previous years, fewer colony-breeding seabirds were affected, and the geographical range of detections was more limited. Further sporadic detections of HPAI A(H5) virus were reported in wild terrestrial carnivores and pinnipeds. Outside Europe, the epidemic continued in the Americas, where also the HPAI A(H7N3) subtype was detected in Mexico. Following its first introduction to mainland Australia, HPAI A(H5N1) virus spread within local wild bird populations and spilled over to terrestrial carnivores and marine mammals. In the US, the number of dairy cattle farms reportedly affected by HPAI A(H5N1) increased, while detections in captive American minks were reported for the first time. Between 5 June and 31 August 2026, 15 cases of avian influenza virus infection were publicly reported in humans (no fatal cases) in three countries and territories: Bangladesh (one A(H5N1) case), Cambodia (one A(H5N1) case) and China (13 A(H9N2) cases). All human cases reported exposure to poultry or a poultry environment prior to detection or onset of illness. Human infections with avian influenza viruses remain rare and no sustained human-to-human transmission has been documented. The risk posed by avian influenza A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b viruses currently circulating in Europe remains low for the general public in the European Union/European Economic Area (EU/EEA) and low-to-moderate for those occupationally or otherwise exposed to infected animals or contaminated environments. ©2026 European Food Safety Authority, European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control,European Union Reference Laboratory for Avian Influenza. EFSA Journal published by Wiley-VCH GmbH on behalf of European Food Safety Authority (Continued . . . ) As the chart at the top of this blog indicates, each avian flu season (which runs Oct 1st -Sept 30th) is different, sometimes punctuated by the arrival of new subtypes or genotypes, and often varying in intensity. As we go into a new fall season, migratory birds in the Northern Hemisphere are expected to bring with them a new wave of HPAI from their high-latitude breeding grounds (see H5Nx: Reassort & Repeat). While we can't know what kind of avian flu season lies ahead, now would be a good time to review the things you can do to lower your (currently, low) risk of exposure. WHO Interim Guidance to Reduce the Risk of Infection in People Exposed to Avian Influenza Viruses Backyard Flock Owners: Protect Yourself from Bird Flu (CDC Guidance) UF/IFAS Extension: What Backyard Flock Owners Need to Know about Bird Flu (Influenza H5N1) Wednesday, September 23, 2026 EM&I: Limited added benefit of seasonal influenza vaccination before A(H5) vaccination in mice and ferrets challenged with A(H5N1) Credit ACIP/CDC #19,345 One of the biggest challenges during any future H5Nx pandemic would be the rapid production and timely deployment of a two-dose (given 30 days apart) H5 vaccine to billions of people (see Referral: SCI AM - A Bird Flu Vaccine Might Come Too Late to Save Us from H5N1). While it's not a new idea (see 2008's Seasonal Flu Vaccine May Offer Some Protection To H5N1), the notion of using the existing seasonal flu vaccine as either a `stop-gap measure' - or as a `prime-boost' for the first pandemic jab, during the opening months of an H5 pandemic - has persisted. An early, encouraging 2010 study in the journal Vaccines (Seasonal influenza vaccine elicits heterosubtypic immunity against H5N1 that can be further boosted by H5N1 vaccination) reported: Recent findings indicate that seasonal influenza vaccination or infection of healthy humans may contribute to heterosubtypic immunity against new influenza A subtypes, such as H5N1. Here, we investigated whether seasonal influenza vaccination in a mouse model could induce any immunity against the H5N1 subtype. It could be demonstrated that, largely due to the H1N1 component strain A/NewCaledonia/20/99, parenteral immunization of mice with a trivalent seasonal influenza vaccine elicited heterosubtype H5-reactive antibodies able to confer partial protection against H5N1 influenza virus infection. Furthermore, the trivalent seasonal influenza vaccine was found to be compatible with a whole virus H5N1 vaccine in a heterologous prime-boost immunization regimen, achieving superior efficacy compared to a single immunization with an equivalent low-dose of the H5N1 vaccine. More recent evidence remains both mixed and modest - and has often relied on ferret or mouse models (which may not fully apply to humans) - including: Nature Comms: Adjuvanted Influenza Vaccination Increases Pre-existing H5N1 Cross-reactive Antibodies mBio: Low levels of influenza H5N1 HA and NA antibodies in the human population are boosted by seasonal H1N1 infection but not by H3N2 infection or influenza vaccination EID Journal: Effect of Seasonal Influenza Vaccines on Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Clade 2.3.4.4b Virus Infection in Ferrets EID Journal: Investigation of Influenza A(H5N1) Virus Neutralization by Quadrivalent Seasonal Vaccines, United Kingdom, 2021–2024 Note: Regardless of whether the seasonal flu vaccine directly protects against H5N1 infection, there are still good reasons to get the jab, prior to - and even during - an H5Nx pandemic. It still may provide some small boost to your immune response. Neutralizing antibodies aren't the only immune defense against infection. It could help prevent a co-infection with H5N1 and seasonal flu, which has the potential for being more severe. Co-infections could also help generate a reassorted `hybrid' virus (see Preprint: Intelligent Prediction & Biological Validation of the High Reassortment Potential of Avian H5N1 and Human H3N2 Influenza Viruses). While it may not be the last word on the topic, today we've a study in EM&I from researchers at the CDC's NCIRD Influenza Division, which frankly, offers little encouragement on the effectiveness of using seasonal flu vaccines as a `prime-boost' for H5N1 vaccines. H5N1 HPAI is a viral disease that impacts both wild and domestic bird populations. Smith Published: Sep. 22, 2026 at 9:12 PM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google TEXAS (KAUZ) - Following a catastrophic strain of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in 2025 that resulted in tens of millions of birds being culled, egg prices soared. Texas A&M AgriLife is reporting that researchers from their College of Agriculture and Life Sciences are preparing to test a new potential line of defense, a form of ultraviolet light called far-UVC, to see if it can kill HPAI without harming birds on poultry farms. Far-UVC light differs from conventional germicidal UV light because it can inactivate viruses and bacteria without penetrating deeply enough to damage human or animal skin and eyes. Researchers will use air-sampling equipment to measure indicator organisms, including aerobic bacteria, coliforms and Staphylococcus aureus, before and after far-UVC exposure. Those readings will inform far-UVC’s potential impact on pathogens like HPAI, according to Texas A&M AgriLife. The project is funded through a $2 million U.S. Department of Agriculture Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service grant from the Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza Poultry Innovation Grand Challenge award. Both times, he had to put down his flock and start over. "My whole business was down for seven months. We just now got back to full capacity," Vlaminck said. Now the virus is back. After a quiet summer, new avian influenza cases are being reported across Minnesota. This month alone, poultry producers in at least five counties have been hit, and more than 200,000 birds have been affected. "And I don't want to go through another shutdown like that," Vlaminck said. Wild birds such as ducks and geese can spread the virus during fall migration, and Vlaminck uses lasers to keep them away from his farm. He bought his first one after avian influenza tore through his operation in 2023, and told WCCO in early 2025 that the lasers had cut his mortality rate roughly in half. But he's also worried that people are moving the virus around. Fall festivals and agritourism draw visitors to places that keep "guinea fowl, chickens, pheasants, ducks, geese, turkeys," Vlaminck said. He and other Minnesota turkey growers are pushing the U.S. Department of Agriculture to move quickly on a vaccination plan for their birds. Vlaminck made the same case to WCCO last October, after bird flu forced him to depopulate about 33,000 birds at one site and roughly 38,000 at another. Growers say the numbers back them up. The number of turkeys raised in the U.S. has fallen from 240 million to 195 million over the past 10 years. Since 2022, nearly 23 million turkeys nationwide have been put down because of the virus. "We are raising fewer birds, but we are also destroying just as many as we ever have, if not more, because of avian influenza," Vlaminck said. Minnesota is the nation's top turkey-producing state, and more than 10 million commercial birds there have been lost to bird flu since 2022, WCCO reported in June. University of Minnesota researchers said then that the virus is likely endemic, meaning it could be a problem for years. Vlaminck and his employees have had to destroy their own flock twice, and they're doing what they can to keep it from happening again. "When something like this comes around and we have to destroy the birds, and they don't make it to market, it's just very disheartening. It's very hard on all our employees and our mental health," he said. Minnesota turkey growers say turkey bought in stores is safe to eat. Birds infected with bird flu do not enter the food supply. (Photo: Polly Sadler, Unsplash) FARGO, N.D. — The fall migratory bird season has arrived, bringing an increased risk of transmission of highly pathogenic avian influenza to domestic birds. On Sept. 1, a commercial turkey operation in LaMoure County, North Dakota, was confirmed to have HPAI. This is the first recorded case in North Dakota this fall. Both commercial producers and owners of backyard flocks should review and implement biosecurity protocols to reduce disease transmission from wild birds to domestic birds or livestock, according to North Dakota State University Extension specialists. “HPAI is a disease carried by wild birds that can affect domestic birds and livestock,” explains Dr. Jake Galbreath, NDSU Extension veterinarian. “Avian influenza is caused by a Type A influenza virus, which is shed in feces and respiratory secretions of infected birds and can survive for weeks in cool, damp environments.” Migration can be followed via BirdCast (https://birdcast.info/), an online real-time migration prediction tool. Biosecurity in domestic flocks Most cases in domestic animals involve poultry and dairy cattle. However, cases have been documented in other mammals, such as goats and pigs. Cats can develop severe, fatal illness if exposed. For reducing transmission between wildlife and domestic birds, Dr. Galbreath recommends the following: If possible, keep poultry or livestock housed until the risk for transmission has decreased. Nonlethal methods to deter wildlife are available on the U.S. Department of Agriculture Wildlife Service’s nonlethal initiative webpage: https://www.aphis.usda.gov/wildlife-services/about/nonlethal. Reduce the attractiveness for wildlife to visit the property by cleaning up litter and spilled feed around domestic flock housing. After coming into contact with or handling wildlife, change into clean clothes, wash hands and disinfect footwear before contact with domestic animals. Report sick or dead wildlife to the North Dakota Game and Fish Department at https://bit.ly/mortality-report. In the event of carcass disposal or handling to reduce potential interactions, follow the appropriate procedures: ndsu.ag/NDSU-HPAI-26. The best defense against HPAI is having a biosecurity plan in place, according to Mary Keena, NDSU Extension livestock environmental management specialist. “It is your job as an animal owner to create a line of separation between your clean animals and the potentially unclean issues that wildlife or visitors may bring,” says Keena. For reducing transmission between domestic animals, Keena recommends the following: Restrict access to property and animals. Allow contact from people who care for the animals, but minimize visitors. After being near other animals or animal owners — such as at feed stores — clean and disinfect the vehicle and its tires. New animals should be kept separate from the flock or herd for at least 30 days. Do not share lawn and garden equipment, tools or supplies with a neighbor or other flock/herd owners. Biosecurity during fall hunting season Hunters participating in fall bird and deer season should be aware of the risk of HPAI in wildlife and take steps to prevent transmission to domestic poultry or livestock. Dr. Galbreath recommends considering implementing the following biosecurity practices: Do not haul disease home. After being out walking in fields or wetlands while hunting, be sure to change clothing and footwear before crossing the clean/dirty line to care for animals. Do not walk through or drive trucks, tractors or equipment through areas where waterfowl or other wildlife feces may be. If this is unavoidable, clean any footwear, vehicles and equipment thoroughly. Field dress game birds when possible to reduce the potential for disease transfer. Plucking/skinning should be done in the field, with feathers properly bagged and disposed of before returning to a site with domestic birds. Knives, coolers and other equipment should be washed with disinfecting soap away from sites where birds have access and allowed to thoroughly dry. More information about biosecurity is available on the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s H5N1 Influenza page: https://www.aphis.usda.gov/h5n1-hpai. While the transmission rate from animals to humans is low, HPAI is a zoonotic disease. Miranda Meehan, NDSU Extension livestock environmental stewardship specialist and disaster education coordinator, reminds owners that animals testing positive for HPAI are prohibited by law from entering the commercial marketplace. “Avian influenza is not a food safety issue when consuming properly cooked meat or eggs and commercial dairy products, which are pasteurized,” says Meehan. “However, there is a risk to individuals consuming raw milk, raw milk cheese and other raw dairy products from cattle that have been exposed to HPAI.” In 2026, six positive HPAI cases in domestic birds or poultry have been reported in North Dakota, with no cases in dairy reported. records.content: 孟加拉国商业鹌鹑中新出现的高致病性禽流感病毒A(H5N1)2.3.4.4b分支:基因重组与公共卫生风险 《Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses》:Emergence of Novel Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza Virus A(H5N1) Clade 2.3.4.4b in Commercial Poultry, Bangladesh 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年09月23日 来源:Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses 3.9 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 ORIGINAL ARTICLE Open Access **背景** 高致病性禽流感(high-pathogenicity avian influenza,HPAI)病毒是对动物与人类健康、家禽生产力及生态系统的主要威胁。新进化的A(H5N1)2.3.4.4b分支病毒因其不断扩展的多宿主生态(包括家禽及广泛的哺乳动物物种)而成为全球关注的焦点。 **方法** 研究人员从暴发严重呼吸道症状和高死亡率的商业鹌鹑养殖场中分离出禽流感病毒(avian influenza virus,AIV)。通过全基因组测序技术和系统发育分析对所检出病毒进行了分子特征鉴定。 **结果** 遗传与系统发育分析显示,该病毒的血凝素(hemagglutinin,HA)基因与孟加拉国活禽市场(live bird markets,LBMs)中近期流行的HPAI A(H5N1)2.3.4.4b毒株紧密聚集,其最近共同祖先可追溯至2023年7月。NA基因及四个内部基因(PB1、NP、MP、NS)源自LBM鸭群中流行的A(H5N1)病毒,而PB2和PA片段则与低致病性禽流感(low pathogenicity avian influenza,LPAI)病毒具有相似性,提示禽类宿主体内发生了基因重配事件。该病毒具有多碱性切割位点(PLREKRRKR↓GLF)、禽类特异性受体结合残基(Q224和G226)及五个保守糖基化基序,与高致病性表型和强禽类受体亲和力一致。PB2基因携带罕见的I147T替换,但关键哺乳动物适应标记(如E627K和D701N)不存在。 **结论** 这种具有高致病性并与LBM来源毒株存在遗传关联的重配A(H5N1)2.3.4.4b病毒目前正在孟加拉国商业家禽种群中传播,增加了病毒适应、跨物种传播的潜力,并对家禽行业和公共卫生构成威胁。 **论文解读** 安捷伦Seahorse XF Pro细胞分析仪:高精度实时测量活细胞耗氧率、细胞外酸化率。欢迎领取细胞能量代谢分析产品资料 领 取 **一、研究背景与科学问题** 禽流感病毒(avian influenza virus,AIV)属于正黏病毒科(*Orthomyxoviridae*),是有包膜的单股负链RNA病毒。其表面的血凝素(hemagglutinin,HA)和神经氨酸酶(neuraminidase,NA)两种主要糖蛋白是亚型分类的基础。H5和H7亚型常与高致病性禽流感(high-pathogenicity avian influenza,HPAI)毒株相关,对家禽具有增强的感染性和毒力,偶尔也感染人类。1996年在中国首次出现的A(H5N1)鹅/广东/1/96(Gs/GD)谱系引发了2003年全球家禽大流行。此后,A(H5Nx)病毒通过与其他禽流感病毒基因重配不断演化,形成了超过30个不同的分支和亚分支,展现了显著的遗传可塑性和全球传播能力。自2016年以来,H5Nx 2.3.4.4b分支病毒的出现和全球蔓延导致广泛的病毒多样性,并最终在野鸟中形成地方性流行。HPAI A(H5N1) 2.3.4.4b已造成全球100多个国家超过11400起鸡形目(*Galliformes*)疫情,并已跨种传播至多种哺乳动物,包括野生和圈养食肉动物、海洋哺乳动物,以及近期的奶牛(包括持续牛传牛传播)。该分支因其增强的基因重配能力、在禽类宿主中的高效传播,以及不断增加的跨物种屏障能力而尤为令人担忧,已被世界卫生组织列入人畜共患流感候选疫苗病毒(candidate vaccine viruses,CVVs)清单。 孟加拉国于2007年2月首次报告家禽HPAI A/H5N1暴发。截至2025年6月,世界动物卫生组织已累计报告586起养殖家禽疫情,涉及H5分支2.2、2.2.2、2.2.3、2.3.2、2.3.4、2.3.4.2和2.3.2.1a,但自2012年以来仅在家禽中检出2.3.2.1a分支。然而,自2016年以来,在孟加拉国活禽市场(live bird markets,LBMs)的鸭子及野鸟中检出了A(H5N1) 2.3.4.4h和A(H5N6) 2.3.4.4b分支病毒,表明病毒持续引入、重配和在外界禽类生态系统中隐匿循环。自1990年以来,鹌鹑养殖已成为孟加拉国蓬勃发展的产业,具有重要的经济价值。研究认为鹌鹑是鸭病毒在陆禽中的中间宿主,比其他鸡形目家禽更易感染源自水禽的禽流感病毒。鉴于鹌鹑对流感病毒的易感性和在市场链条中与其他家禽品种的频繁混合,其可能作为中间宿主促进病毒适应和跨种传播。然而,孟加拉国集约化养殖鹌鹑中HPAI感染的报告仍然有限。本研究首次报告了与孟加拉国商业鹌鹑养殖场严重暴发相关的HPAI A(H5N1) 2.3.4.4b病毒的检出和遗传特征鉴定,并评估了其与当前其他物种中流行病毒的相关性。 **二、研究设计与技术方法** 研究人员于2024年10月至2025年2月期间,从孟加拉国达卡专区Savar分区的四个不同商业鹌鹑养殖场采集了32份口咽和泄殖腔拭子样本(每场8份,来自4只垂死鹌鹑)。这些养殖场均未接种H5或H9禽流感疫苗,群体规模为1000-5000只,年龄40-180天不等,每场在临床症状出现48小时内死亡率均超过40%。研究采用的方法主要包括:(1)通过实时逆转录聚合酶链反应(real-time reverse transcriptase PCR,RT-qPCR)对样本进行禽流感病毒M基因筛查和H5/N1亚型确认;(2)利用9-11日龄无特定病原体(specific pathogen-free,SPF)鸡胚进行病毒分离;(3)采用Illumina NextSeq 2000平台进行下一代测序(next-generation sequencing,NGS)获得全基因组序列;(4)使用MAFFT、IQ-Tree2和TreeTime等工具进行系统发育分析和时间缩放进化树推断;(5)通过Nextclade和FluMut等平台进行氨基酸突变分析,重点关注切割位点、受体结合位点和潜在N-连接糖基化基序;(6)对自然感染鹌鹑的胰腺、肺、前胃、脾脏和十二指肠等组织进行苏木精-伊红(hematoxylin and eosin,H&E)染色组织病理学检查。 **三、主要研究结果** **3.1 HPAI病毒的检测与分离** 在采集的32份样本中,所有样本经实时RT-qPCR检测均为A(H5N1)禽流感病毒阳性,循环阈值(Ct值)范围为16-31,表明样本间病毒载量存在差异。经RT-PCR确认后,病毒分离尝试中共从11份样本成功分离出活病毒,接种后72小时内出现鸡胚死亡证实了病毒复制,收获的尿囊液血凝试验(HA)阳性。 **3.2 组织病理学病变** 对感染HPAI的鹌鹑的组织病理学检查显示与系统性病毒播散一致的严重多系统病变。肺表现为显著充血、出血、肺水肿、弥漫性炎性细胞浸润伴有间质增厚和气腔部分闭塞;胰腺出现腺泡细胞广泛凝固性坏死,正常结构丧失,伴血管充血和轻度炎性浸润;脑部出现符合脑炎的病变,以胶质细胞增生和微脓肿形成为特征,偶见脑膜炎;气管表现为气管炎,伴有腺体增生和炎性改变。 **3.3 系统发育相关性** HA基因的系统发育分析显示,该病毒与亚洲其他H5 2.3.4.4b序列相似,特别是与孟加拉国达卡和吉大港LBM的样本关系最为密切,这些样本采集于2023-2024年间,最近共同祖先时间可追溯至2023年7月。其他七个病毒基因片段的系统发育分析发现,PB1、NP、NA、MP和NS片段与2023-2024年LBM鸭源的A(H5N1) 2.3.4.4b病毒相似。值得注意的是,PB2和PA片段除与孟加拉国其他A/H5 2.3.4.4b病毒相似外,还与韩国和孟加拉国检出的非H5低致病性禽流感(low pathogenicity avian influenza,LPAI)病毒H4N6、H6N3和H1N2具有相似性,提示已存在的H5 2.3.4.4b HPAI病毒与该地区流行LPAI病毒之间发生了重配事件。一株2024年采自孟加拉国LBM鸭子的A(H5N1) 2.3.4.4b序列(A/duck/Bangladesh/64227/2024)与A/quail/Bangladesh/3-25H/2024在所有系统发育树中均聚集在一起。Clustal Omega分析显示两株病毒在所有基因片段上的核苷酸同一性为98.69%-99.80%,表明这一特定基因组合可能正在孟加拉国流行但目前尚未被充分检测。此外,在NS、PB1和NP系统发育树中,若干H5 2.3.2.1a序列与A/quail/Bangladesh/3-25H/2024聚集成群,表明孟加拉国流行的两种主要H5 HPAI分支在家禽种群中持续存在并发生基因片段交换。 **3.4 基因组分析** Highly pathogenic avian influenza detected in Boone County

by Cami Koons, Iowa Capital Dispatch
September 22, 2026

The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship confirmed a case of the highly pathogenic avian influenza in Boone County, marking the state’s seventh detection of the bird flu in 2026.

The outbreak occurred in a backyard, mixed species flock of 138 birds, according to IDALS.

Iowa has not reported a case of the H5N1 bird flu since March, when it logged two backyard flock outbreaks. None of the 2026 outbreaks in Iowa have been in commercial poultry flocks.

The current outbreak of the highly pathogenic avian flu started in February 2022 and since then has impacted more than 30 million birds in Iowa and more than 208 million birds nationally, according to the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service with the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

IDALS urged poultry owners to continue “bolstering” their biosecurity practices and to contact their veterinarians immediately if they suspect birds are sick with the virus.

That is according to data from the Board of Animal Health. Three outbreaks were reported from September 10 through the 15 impacting over 118,000 birds, including at a pair of turkey operations in Big Stone and Becker County. There was also some reported and at a poultry breeder in Otter Tail County. The Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota is reporting that 16 flocks have tested positive for highly pathogenic avian influenza in the past 30 days. That impacts roughly 400,000 birds statewide. The issue facing producers is the spread of Avian flu from wild birds is something that's almost unpreventable, according to Shauna Voss with the Minnesota Board of Animal Health. "During our spring and fall migrations when birds start to move, it kind of kicks off new outbreaks as the wild birds are carrying the virus with them," says Voss. "And then it does occasionally spill over into our domestic poultry populations despite some of our best efforts that we are using to try to control it." The flu is fatal and can wipe out an entire flock in days but Voss says it doesn't put a producer out of commission. "While it does mean the end of that flock, that does not mean that that producer is out of commission," she says. "They do have to go through virus elimination activities to make sure that the virus isn't contained on their farm, but then once they've met all of those requirements, they are allowed to restock with birds and start over." Voss adds that while it can be alarming, the state and federal government have resources to help. "We work well as a team in Minnesota with our USDA colleagues, with our Minnesota Department of Ag colleagues, with the Board of Animal Health and the producers to make sure that we detect these viruses early and take action to prevent it from just spreading uncontrolled within our domestic populations," she explains. So far, the five affected flocks in Minnesota, along with four in South Dakota and one in Wisconsin, North Dakota, Montana and Idaho, are the only reports of Avian Influenza so far in the U.S. over the last 30 days. Last winter, bird flu outbreaks in the U.S. helped drive up the price of eggs and poultry. Minnesota Grocers Association President Patrick Garofalo told WCCO Radio in January that the destruction of those flocks is a primary driver in high prices. "Consumers and businesses are suffering the consequences of this bird flu epidemic and all the chickens that have been slaughtered as a result of it. Prev Next Photo by: MTN News File By: Emily Brown Posted 1:31 AM, Sep 23, 2026 BITTERROOT VALLEY — Last week, bird flu was detected in a commercial flock of chickens in Ravalli County. Tahnee Szymanski, Montana's state veterinarian, tells MTN this is associated with waterfowl migration. "Over the last 30 days in the U.S., the Dakotas, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Idaho, and now Montana have all had detections, which were kind of all in right the same band of latitude across the U.S. And so it's just that time of year when we know that the risk of HPI [Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza] seems to come up," Szymanski said. WATCH: Bird flu detected in Ravalli County commercial chicken flock State veterinarian shares details on bird flu in the Bitterroot Szymanski notes that wild waterfowl can carry the flu without being impacted by symptoms. Those birds often spread the virus by releasing fluids into shared water sources or food supplies. "Additionally, the virus is capable of surviving for a period of time. And so even if the birds are relatively confined, and a person goes out and goes into a contaminated environment, they could potentially move that virus back to their coop," Szymanski shared. In Ravalli County, the illness was detected in an egg-producing flock that lives near a pond. By the time that it was reported to us, they had lost maybe 50 to 60 birds and by the time it was confirmed, I believe that they had lost about 100 birds," Szymanski detailed. "As far as any eggs that have left the premises, they would have been prior to this detection. So, no worry about kind of any potential risk out there in the environment or to the community," she continued. Szymanski says that there are precautions people can take to protect their poultry, including keeping flocks indoors. "We typically say until about the end of December, end of January, depending on what we're seeing kind of at the national level," Szymanski said. "They should secure water sources; they should secure food sources so that wild birds aren't getting into those. They should think about having dedicated clothing and footwear that they can use for their coops.” Szymanski adds that the risk to people is low, but to be cautious, as the virus can linger and be transferred. While the Health Department can’t share the exact location of the sick flock, those living nearby should have received word, and they say to keep an eye on animals. "If you're seeing any illness in your birds, please reach out to us," Szymanski said. records.content_title: H5N1 confirmed in marine mammals in Australia — Mongabay
records.content: News World H5N1 confirmed in marine mammals in Australia — Mongabay UA.NEWS 21 September 2026 08:32 In Australia, the H5N1 bird flu virus is rapidly spreading among wild birds in the southeast of the country and has also been confirmed in several mammal species. According to Mongabay , H5N1 has been detected in South Australia, including in an Australian sea lion and a common dolphin. Cases among mammals At the end of August, H5N1 was detected in a red fox in Adelaide. Acting Chief Veterinary Officer Cameron Bell said that wild foxes do not usually spread the virus directly. At the same time, scavenging animals can move infected carcasses between different habitats. In September, South Australian authorities confirmed H5N1 in an Australian sea lion and a common dolphin. State Environment Minister Emily Bourke said that the sea lion had been recovering from a shark attack when it died from the virus. The species is critically endangered, and its population is declining by about 2% annually. Bird flu was also recorded in long-nosed fur seals in the state. Australia’s first case of H5N1 in a pelican was confirmed on the Yorke Peninsula. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Risks for coastal animals The virus is being detected among little penguins, magpies, crested terns and pelicans. Victoria’s chief biodiversity officer, James Todd, noted that bird congregations during the breeding period are likely to accelerate transmission of the infection to mammals. Bill Bateman, an associate professor of behavioral ecology at Curtin University, suggested that marine mammals are most likely infected by birds. According to him, animals may eat sick or dead seabirds or come into contact with their biological fluids, contaminated water or substrate. Bateman also stressed that safely removing carcasses is important to reduce scavenging animals’ contact with the virus. On the Fleurieu Peninsula, volunteers from the Victor Harbor Dolphin Watch group are monitoring dolphins that display atypical behavior while swimming or have neurological symptoms. Roy Graber September 22, 2026 Roy Graber | DALL-E Article Summary Highly pathogenic avian influenza has infected four commercial poultry flocks in Manitoba in September, with three new cases confirmed on September 21 and 22 in the rural municipalities of Cartier, Rockwood, and Rhineland, making Manitoba the only Canadian province with confirmed HPAI cases since spring. Four Manitoba flocks infected: The first case was confirmed September 10 in De Salaberry, identified as a turkey flock, followed by three additional cases on September 21-22. HPAI locations: New cases confirmed in Cartier, Rockwood, and Rhineland rural municipalities. Canada's only active outbreak: Manitoba remains the sole Canadian province with confirmed HPAI cases since spring; the previous case was May 16 in Alberta. U.S. spread continues: Four American states—Minnesota, South Dakota, North Dakota, and Wisconsin—reported HPAI detections in September. Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) has struck three more commercial poultry flocks in the Canadian province of Manitoba. The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) reported that two of those cases were confirmed Sept. 21, one in the rural municipality of Cartier and the other in Rockwood. The third case was confirmed Sept. 22 in Rhineland. With these three cases, Manitoba has had four commercial poultry flocks affected by HPAI in September. The first case was confirmed Sept. 10 in De Salaberry, and the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) identified that flock as a commercial turkey flock. Neither the CFIA nor WOAH has disclosed what type of poultry was in the three most recently confirmed cases. So far, Manitoba remains the only province to have a confirmed case since spring. Before the September cases in Manitoba, the last case of HPAI in Canadian poultry was confirmed May 16 in Starland County, Alberta. Meanwhile, four U.S. states — Minnesota, South Dakota, North Dakota and Wisconsin — have had confirmed HPAI detections in September.
